content:
The board has welcomed Anishka Jelicich’s commencement. Image supplied

New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) has today announced that Anishka Jelicich has commenced her role as Chief Executive Officer.

She joins the organisation following “a successful international career spanning more than two decades across New Zealand, the United Kingdom and Europe”.

Jelicich said she has had the privilege of seeing New Zealand wine through the eyes of the world during her time working internationally in the global wine and drinks sector.

“Time and again I’ve seen the extraordinary respect our wines, our people and our industry command globally. That perspective has only deepened a connection that is both personal and professional, making it a real privilege to join an organisation that has helped shape one of New Zealand’s great success stories through the leadership of Philip Gregan (recently retired CEO), the NZW board, the NZW team, our members and those who have contributed over many years.

“Today, New Zealand wine is the country’s eighth largest export, generating approximately NZ$2.1 billion annually, with our distinctive, refreshing and sustainable wines enjoyed by consumers in more than 100 markets around the world. My first priority is therefore to listen, learn and spend time with people across the industry, understanding what matters most before we write the next chapter together.”

Chair of New Zealand Winegrowers, Fabian Yukich, said the board is delighted to welcome Jelicich into the role.

“We are very pleased to have Anishka join us as CEO. She brings a deep understanding of the New Zealand wine industry, combined with extensive global experience and strong leadership capability. Her strategic perspective and ability to build alignment across stakeholders will be invaluable as we navigate both the opportunities and challenges ahead for our sector,” Yukich said.

NZW said Jelicich’s appointment comes at an important time for the New Zealand wine industry, with “continued global demand for premium New Zealand wines” making the sector “well positioned for long-term growth” and also to respond to “a range of global and domestic pressures facing growers and winemakers”.

title: Cooks Lot releases handpicked 2025 vintage Chardonnay and Pinot Noir
summary:
Cooks Lot has released its 2025 vintage Orange region Cooks Lot ‘Handpicked’ Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Owner and winemaker Duncan Cook said that, while hand harvesting is more labour-intensive, it is “definitely more selective”. "Our vintage team take a great deal of care working their way through the vineyard, picking each bunch by hand, carefully selecting the best and leaving those bunches that may be damaged or not quite ripe. The result is a higher degree of flavour concentration and balance in the finished wines. It is more expensive, but years of experience have shown the quality speaks for itself.”

The post Cooks Lot releases handpicked 2025 vintage Chardonnay and Pinot Noir appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The grapes for the wines have been handpicked and each bottle retails for RRP $35. Image supplied

Cooks Lot has released its 2025 vintage Orange region Cooks Lot ‘Handpicked’ Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

Owner and winemaker Duncan Cook said that, while hand harvesting is more labour-intensive, it is “definitely more selective”.

“Our vintage team take a great deal of care working their way through the vineyard, picking each bunch by hand, carefully selecting the best and leaving those bunches that may be damaged or not quite ripe. The result is a higher degree of flavour concentration and balance in the finished wines. It is more expensive, but years of experience have shown the quality speaks for itself.

“In the winery, our ‘Handpicked’ wines are crafted with complexity in mind. The wines see more new oak and extended maturation. The objective is to produce wines that showcase the region’s fruit purity, with greater depth, length, texture and complexity upon release, while also offering longevity in the cellar.

“We aim to create a more layered palate, enhanced structure, and a higher level of refinement than the ‘Allotment’ range.

“After many years in the kitchen championing fresh produce and proteins, winemaking shares many aspects. My underlying challenge is to hero the variety and the region with the finished wine. Using various winemaking techniques, including barrel selection and maturation time, should create the pedestal and hone the focus that ensures they shine.

The 2025 Cooks Lot ‘Handpicked’ Chardonnay is barrel fermented with partial solids “to build complexity and texture, balancing the lovely concentration and varietal expression of the Orange region fruit”. Cooks Lot said it is aged on its lees, with regular stirring, in a combination of new and one-year-old French oak barriques.

The 2025 Cooks Lot ‘Handpicked’ Pinot Noir is made from a combination of MV6 and 777 clones grown in vineyards sitting at an average elevation above 900m.

“The Pinot Noir was fermented in small open fermenters, with a small component as whole bunches, by wild yeast and gently hand plunged four times a day. This is gentle on the skins, while building complexity and flavour extraction. It also allows us to carefully monitor the ferment,” said Cook.

The free-run juice and pressings were “barrelled separately and matured in tightly grained French oak puncheons for 12 months, prior to blending and bottling”.

Retailing for RRP $35 each, the wines are available here via the Cooks Lot website.

content:
The Great Australian Shiraz Challenge has revealed its 2026 judging line-up and challenge sponsors.

“We are delighted to have Jen Pfeiffer returning as chair, she will be joined by Liz Heidenreich, Katie Spain, Tyson Bitter, Steve Paul and Justin Purser,” said event director Julian McLean.

Fowles Wines will again host this year’s event, with entries opening online Monday 3 August and closing Friday 4 September.

Judging will take place over three days from Tuesday 29 September to Thursday 1 October and winners will be announced online Monday 2 November.

Organisers said that the challenge is a “unique opportunity for Australia’s premier red winemakers to showcase their Shiraz, benchmark winemaking and regional points of differences and assist with reinforcing the reputation of the variety as a national and international wine icon”.

The challenge has been going for 32 years, with wines “classed and tasted based on climate and regional points of difference”. Organisers say this helps ensure all entries are “judged fairly and objectively”.

The award categories have expanded over the competition’s years of operating. In 2016, individual state-based trophies and the award for ‘Best Shiraz Over 5 Years Old’ were introduced. In 2021, the ‘Best Organic Shiraz Trophy’ acknowledged winemakers’ commitment to the category, and a ‘Best Sparkling Shiraz’ class was even introduced in 2022.

Saint Martin Oak returns as the naming rights sponsor, with support also from Orora Glass, MCC Label Solutions, Winetitles Media, Sanector, Melbourne Royal and Interpack.

title: New Zealand Winegrowers ready to celebrate International Pinot Noir Day
summary:
As consumers increasingly seek lighter, fresher wine styles that suit modern lifestyles, New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) says the country’s Pinot Noir is “enjoying a well-deserved moment in the spotlight”. This International Pinot Noir Day (18 August), New Zealand Winegrowers is inviting wine lovers around the world to raise a glass to New Zealand's leading red wine export and “rediscover a variety renowned for its vibrancy, versatility and refreshing appeal”. “New Zealand Pinot Noir is celebrated for its purity, vibrancy and sense of place, offering bright fruit, natural freshness and elegant structure,” said Charlotte Read, general manager brand, New Zealand Winegrowers.

content:
New Zealand Winegrowers is encouraging wine lovers to celebrate International Pinot Noir Day. Image supplied

As consumers increasingly seek lighter, fresher wine styles that suit modern lifestyles, New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) says the country’s Pinot Noir is “enjoying a well-deserved moment in the spotlight”.

This International Pinot Noir Day (18 August), New Zealand Winegrowers is inviting wine lovers around the world to raise a glass to New Zealand’s leading red wine export and “rediscover a variety renowned for its vibrancy, versatility and refreshing appeal”.

“New Zealand Pinot Noir is celebrated for its purity, vibrancy and sense of place, offering bright fruit, natural freshness and elegant structure,” said Charlotte Read, general manager brand, New Zealand Winegrowers.

“It’s one of the world’s most captivating grape varieties because it combines complexity with elegance. New Zealand’s cool climate delivers a distinctive expression, with vibrant fruit, natural freshness and fine tannins that make our Pinot Noir both immediately appealing and incredibly versatile at the table with an array of cuisines around the world.”

The renewed enthusiasm for Pinot Noir also reflects broader trends in the way people are drinking wine, says NZW.

“Consumers are increasingly seeking wines with freshness, balance and drinkability. As a result, Pinot Noir has become one of the most talked-about red wine styles among wine professionals and enthusiasts alike,” the organisation explained.

To mark International Pinot Noir Day, NZW is encouraging wine lovers to share their own ‘Pinot Moments’ on social media using #LoveNZPinot, #NZWine and #PinotNoirDay.

“Whether you’re discovering New Zealand Pinot Noir for the first time or revisiting an old favourite, International Pinot Noir Day is the perfect opportunity to experience why this red continues to capture hearts around the world,” said New Zealand Winegrowers.

title: Wine Australia’s Export Report indicates green shoots despite overall decline
summary:
Australian wine exports declined by 7 per cent in value to $2.30 billion and 6 per cent in volume to 598 million litres in the year ended June 2026, according to Wine Australia’s Export Report released today. This is the first time that export volume has fallen below 600 million litres since 2004. However, Wine Australia said the decline “mirrors a broader global trend of declining wine consumption over the past decade”. Wine Australia explained that worldwide wine consumption has fallen to its lowest level since 1961, as consumers increasingly moderate alcohol intake, face cost-of-living pressures and shift towards alternative beverages. Despite the broader slowdown, Wine Australia flagged several markets which delivered strong growth.

The post Wine Australia’s Export Report indicates green shoots despite overall decline appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Wine Australia has highlighted Canada and Asian markets outside of mainland China as growth areas. Images supplied

Australian wine exports declined by 7 per cent in value to $2.30 billion and 6 per cent in volume to 598 million litres in the year ended June 2026, according to Wine Australia’s Export Report released today.

This is the first time that export volume has fallen below 600 million litres since 2004. However, Wine Australia said the decline “mirrors a broader global trend of declining wine consumption over the past decade”.

Wine Australia explained that worldwide wine consumption has fallen to its lowest level since 1961, as consumers increasingly moderate alcohol intake, face cost-of-living pressures and shift towards alternative beverages.

Figure 1 – Australia wine exports compared to global wine consumption

Wine Australia manager market insights Peter Bailey said the challenges facing Australian wine exporters are not unique, with other wine producing nations facing the same conditions.

“Data from multiple sources suggests the decline in wine consumption globally is more than a short-term downturn – it’s a reflection of changing consumer behaviour that is reshaping demand around the world. This reinforces the importance of understanding where demand exists and the products and occasions that are driving consumer decisions.

“While global trading conditions remain challenging, Australia wine continues to perform relatively well in many key markets where it generally maintained or grew its share of imported wine over the past year,” Bailey said.

According to the organisation, the decline in Australian wine exports for the year ended June 2026 was driven primarily by weaker demand in Australia’s three largest export markets – mainland China, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Mainland China remained Australia’s largest export market by value, despite exports falling 15 per cent to $756 million as the initial post-tariff recovery and restocking phase came to an end.

“While exports to mainland China declined over the past year, Australia remains the leading source of imported wine in the market.

“The market is no longer being driven by the restocking of Australian wine, rather we’re seeing a more mature and demand-led phase, reflecting a smaller and slower-growing Chinese wine market than existed prior to the imposition of tariffs in late 2020,” Bailey added.

The United Kingdom remained Australia’s largest market by volume and the United States second, although export volume to both markets fell to their lowest level in 25 years.

“While trading conditions in the UK remain challenging, Australia continues to hold the leading share of the UK off-trade market, reflecting the long-standing popularity of Australian wine among British consumers. Most of the decline is coming from commercial and mid-priced wines. Higher-value Australian wines have been more resilient and continue to attract demand in the UK market.

“Unlike the UK, where premium wines have remained relatively resilient, the US data points to weaker demand across most price categories. This suggests Australia’s challenges in the US extend beyond entry-level wines and reflect wider market headwinds, including declining wine consumption, increased competition from domestic and imported producers, retailer inventory reductions, and changing consumer preferences toward alternative alcoholic beverages,” Bailey said.

Despite the broader slowdown, Wine Australia flagged several markets which delivered strong growth.

“Canada was a standout performer, with export value increasing 20 per cent to $188 million – its highest level in seven years – and volume rising 13 per cent. This growth stands out against a backdrop of declining wine consumption generally in Canada, with Australia’s growth supported by market-share gains following reduced availability of US wines during the Canada–US trade dispute. This growth momentum softened towards the end of the period suggesting this market-share gain is beginning to stabilise.

“Asian markets outside mainland China also delivered strong growth. Export value increased significantly in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. Singapore became Australia’s largest Asian market outside of mainland China, while Thailand achieved record export values driven by growing demand for premium Australian wines,” Bailey concluded.

Figure 2 – Value of exports to key Asian destinations (excluding mainland China)

The top five markets by value were:

  • Mainland China, down 15 per cent to $756 million.
  • United Kingdom, down 3 per cent to $340 million.
  • United States, down 27 per cent to $229 million.
  • Canada, up 20 per cent to $188 million.
  • Singapore, up 11 per cent to $125 million.

 

The top five markets by volume were:

  • United Kingdom, down 6 per cent to 192 million litres.
  • United States, down 15 per cent to 95 million litres.
  • Mainland China, down 8 per cent to 77 million litres.
  • Canada, up 13 per cent to 69 million litres.
  • New Zealand, up 1 per cent to 26 million litres.

title: Art Gallery of NSW to take on official wine partner, increases local wine offerings
summary:
A spokesperson for the Art Gallery of NSW has confirmed that its business development team is currently inviting expressions of interest from wineries interested in becoming the official wine partner of the Art Gallery. “Commencing in December 2026, the Art Gallery is seeking to establish a new multi-year partnership valued between $150,000 and $200,000 per annum in combined cash and in-kind support. The opportunity is aimed at a wine brand of the highest standard that wishes to demonstrate its commitment to supporting the arts.” The decision comes after the Art Gallery of NSW received criticism earlier this month from NSW producers over having more interstate wines on the menu at its restaurants. Since then, the spokesperson explained that the gallery has expanded its offerings of local wines. The issue was originally raised by Orange-based wine advocate David Cumming, who welcomed the change.

The post Art Gallery of NSW to take on official wine partner, increases local wine offerings appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
Exterior view of the Art Gallery of New South Wales. Image credit Iwan Baan.

By Kyra Trussell

A spokesperson for the Art Gallery of NSW has confirmed that its business development team is currently inviting expressions of interest from wineries interested in becoming the official wine partner of the Art Gallery.

“Commencing in December 2026, the Art Gallery is seeking to establish a new multi-year partnership valued between $150,000 and $200,000 per annum in combined cash and in-kind support. The opportunity is aimed at a wine brand of the highest standard that wishes to demonstrate its commitment to supporting the arts.

“In line with relevant policies and guidelines, we note that sponsorship of the Art Gallery does not guarantee retail representation at the Art Gallery’s onsite food and beverage outlets. The Fresh Collective, the Art Gallery’s catering partner, is responsible for making its own independent commercial decisions regarding the products it stocks and serves,” the spokesperson explained to Daily Wine News.

The decision comes after the Art Gallery of NSW received criticism earlier this month from NSW producers over having more interstate wines on the menu at its restaurants.

Since then, the spokesperson explained that the gallery has expanded its offerings of local wines.

“Separately, we can advise that the Art Gallery recently asked The Fresh Collective to explore ways to further support NSW wine producers. As a result, since 22 July 2026, The Fresh Collective has expanded its NSW wine offering, with NSW wines now accounting for 50% of the selection at MOD Dining and 44% of the wine offering at the Gallery Café.”

The issue was originally raised by Orange-based wine advocate David Cumming, who welcomed the change.

“It’s great to see a move from the Art Gallery of NSW to build a better presence of the state’s wines within the gallery. This is a very positive step forward, and 50% NSW in MOD shows a strong example of the support that can be achieved. It would be good to see this emulated in the ‘Crafted by Mat Moran’ restaurant in the gallery,” Cumming said.

As for the partnership, Cumming believes the offering could have been more accessible to smaller wineries.

“With regard to the sponsorship, it is nice to see NSW in focus. However, given the size of many family-owned winemakers in the state, there are not many that can offer this sort of marketing budget, especially as it does not involve further purchase of the sponsors’ wines in the gallery. This is a missed opportunity and shows a bit of a lack of understanding of the NSW wine sector,” he said.

Cumming said supporters of the movement would still like to see the NSW government go further in supporting winegrowers across all publicly owned venues.

“It needs to be a lasting commitment, one that isn’t reliant on who is managing a venue at the time, but a government initiative that says we support NSW winegrowers. This will hopefully give wine distributors further confidence in having more NSW brands in their portfolio and subsequently broadening the wines across Sydney and beyond.

“This could be as simple as developing lease agreements for caterers and businesses operating out of NSW-owned venues, requiring a percentage of NSW wines be listed. We’re not asking for grants or funding. It is a no-cost change for government.

“There is a fantastic opportunity to do this with the upcoming opening of the $900M Powerhouse Museum in Parramatta,” Cumming said.

Expressions of interest for the partnership should be submitted via email to businessdevelopment@ag.nsw.gov.au by Friday 14 August 2026. The spokesperson for the Art Gallery of NSW noted that “any partnership will be subject to the art gallery’s due diligence processes, the NSW Government Sponsorship Policy and the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (ICAC) sponsorship guidelines”.

To “help ensure NSW wine producers are aware of the opportunity”, the gallery spokesperson said NSW Wine and Wine Australia have been notified and invited to share the information with their members.

title: Coonawarra wines to hit the road this August
summary:
Producers from Coonawarra in South Australia will be taking their wines on a tour across the country this August as a part of the annual Coonawarra Wine Tasting Roadshow. With tastings to be held in Adelaide, Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and the Sunshine Coast, the annual Roadshow will see up to 20 Coonawarra producers travel “from the famed Terra Rossa soils of regional South Australia to bring the region's wines directly to consumers”. The event is celebrating 23 years in 2026, with more than 15,000 Coonawarra wines having been poured across 125 roadshow events since its inception in 2003. Heidi Guyett, events and marketing manager at Coonawarra Vignerons, said the roadshow is a fantastic opportunity to connect directly with the region’s winemakers.

The post Coonawarra wines to hit the road this August appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The 23rd Coonawarra Wine Tasting Roadshow is set for August 2026. Image supplied

Producers from Coonawarra in South Australia will be taking their wines on a tour across the country this August as a part of the annual Coonawarra Wine Tasting Roadshow.

With tastings to be held in Adelaide, Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and the Sunshine Coast, the annual Roadshow will see up to 20 Coonawarra producers travel “from the famed Terra Rossa soils of regional South Australia to bring the region’s wines directly to consumers”.

The event is celebrating 23 years in 2026, with more than 15,000 Coonawarra wines having been poured across 125 roadshow events since its inception in 2003.

Heidi Guyett, events and marketing manager at Coonawarra Vignerons, said the roadshow is a fantastic opportunity to connect directly with the region’s winemakers.

“There’s something special about meeting the people behind the wines – hearing their stories, learning about vintages and discovering the character that makes Coonawarra so unique,” said Guyett.

Coonawarra Vignerons said that anywhere between 100 and 150 wines will be poured at the tasting events “with a great range of varieties and styles up for tasting”.

“The cool climatic conditions of the Coonawarra Wine Region make for outstanding white wines that are crisp and aromatic. From Riesling to Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris – there will be something for every wine lover – sparkling wines included,” Guyett explained.

Emma Raidis from Raidis Estate said the roadshow is one of the highlights of the year for Coonawarra producers.

“We love the Coonawarra Roadshow because it’s about so much more than pouring wine. It’s about meeting people face-to-face, sharing a laugh, telling our family’s story and showing why we’re so passionate about Coonawarra.

“Seeing the enthusiasm people have for our region reminds us why we do what we do, and we always leave with new friendships and great memories.”

Raidis added that the roadshow is “just as rewarding for the wineries as it is for the people attending”.

“It’s also a wonderful opportunity to catch up with our mates from home. Everyone is always a little more excited when they see the bright lights of the city! There’s a real sense of camaraderie amongst the wineries — it’s a bit like school camp for winemakers.”

Coonawarra Vignerons said a highlight of the roadshow will be the return to the Starship Sydney for an afternoon cruise on the water at Sydney Harbour.

“We’re thrilled to be returning to Sydney Harbour for a second year,” said Guyett.

“The response to last year’s event was outstanding. There’s something truly special about enjoying Coonawarra wines while cruising past some of Australia’s most iconic landmarks. It’s a relaxed afternoon of exceptional wine, wonderful company and unforgettable views.

“Guests can chat directly with our winemakers, discover new favourites and experience the warmth and hospitality of Coonawarra in one of Sydney’s most spectacular settings.”

Tickets are now on sale for all five Roadshow events. Tickets include “event entry, souvenir RIEDEL wine glass, three hours of unlimited wine tastings, complimentary food offerings and the opportunity to meet the makers behind Coonawarra’s world-class wines”.

title: Two new directors appointed to Wine Australia Board
summary:
The federal government has announced that two new directors have been appointed to the Wine Australia Board. Darryn Hakof and Stephen Strachan have been appointed for three-year terms and are set to “help strengthen Wine Australia’s role in supporting Australia’s wine sector to respond to emerging opportunities and challenges across domestic and international markets”. The government said the appointments will “ensure Wine Australia has the leadership and expertise needed to support industry through this period of transition and opportunity”. Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Julie Collins MP, said that the two bring valuable skills, experience and industry knowledge. “These new directors will help Wine Australia support grapegrowers and winemakers to respond to current challenges and new opportunities in domestic and export markets.” Australian Grape & Wine (AGW) has welcomed the appointment of the two directors.

The post Two new directors appointed to Wine Australia Board appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The federal government has announced that two new directors have been appointed to the Wine Australia Board.

Darryn Hakof and Stephen Strachan have been appointed for three-year terms and are set to “help strengthen Wine Australia’s role in supporting Australia’s wine sector to respond to emerging opportunities and challenges across domestic and international markets”.

The government said the appointments will “ensure Wine Australia has the leadership and expertise needed to support industry through this period of transition and opportunity”.

Strachan is said to bring “extensive industry knowledge, a practical understanding of the opportunities and challenges facing Australian wine producers, and a strong track record of collaboration across industry and government”.

Meanwhile, Hakof contributes his “significant international and commercial expertise, including experience in market development, market access and global industry engagement, further enhancing the board’s strategic outlook and global industry connections”.

Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Julie Collins MP, said that the two bring valuable skills, experience and industry knowledge.

“These new directors will help Wine Australia support grapegrowers and winemakers to respond to current challenges and new opportunities in domestic and export markets.”

She added that the government “has delivered over $90 million in funding to support the grape and wine sector, acknowledging how critical this industry is to Australia”.

Expanding the board from five to seven members “also brings Wine Australia into line with other research and development corporations, strengthening its capacity, governance and industry expertise at a time of significant change for Australia’s wine sector”, according to the government.

Dr Michele Allan will continue as acting chair, while recruitment of a permanent chair is finalised.

Australian Grape & Wine (AGW) has welcomed the appointment of the two directors.

“Mr Hakof and Mr Strachan bring a wealth of wine industry experience, strong commercial expertise and a genuine passion for Australian wine” said Helen Strachan, chair of AGW.

“These appointments will further strengthen the breadth of skills and experience around the board table and provide valuable leadership as the industry works through one of the most significant periods of structural adjustment in generations”.

”We look forward to working with Mr Hakof and Mr Strachan, together with the broader Wine Australia Board, to support a sustainable and profitable future for Australia’s grape and wine sector.”

Strachan also acknowledged the extension of Allan’s acting chair position.

“The appointment of a permanent chair is an important decision for both Wine Australia and the broader industry. We appreciate the government taking the time to ensure the right appointment is made and look forward to working with the successful candidate once that process is complete.”

content:
1933-1935 Wine judging with Arthur Kelman pictured far right. Image supplied

Judging is now underway for the milestone 200th edition of the Sydney Royal Wine Show.

1500 wines will be assessed by “30 of Australia’s best judges” as well as international guest judge Matthew Jukes from the United Kingdom.

Over the next four days, a total of 10,000 glasses will be poured, with wines judged across 55 different classes.

In 1826, during its fourth annual agricultural exhibition, the Agricultural Society of NSW offered a small gold medal for the best sample of colonial wine – at least 10 gallons, certified on oath to be from that year’s vintage.

By 1828, there were four classes for wine, despite the colony only having a handful of serious growers. The show system had started small but gained momentum. By 1901, a purpose-built exhibition space called ‘the wine kiosk’ was being built at the Agricultural Society of NSW’s home at Moore Park, giving exhibitors the chance to showcase their wines.

Following judging, the RAS will host an industry symposium on 31 July titled ‘Sydney Royal 200: The Wine Show Conversation’, which will offer “robust discussion around the history and value of wine shows in Australia and where they are heading”.

Trophy winners of the 2026 Sydney Royal Wine Show will then be announced at an awards lunch on 21 August.
